evidence.claim: A former toll road crosses mountains once contested by Civil War armies.
evidence.quote: Engineered by Claudius Crozet through the mountainous terrain, it was a toll road partially funded by the Virginia Board of Public Works. Control of this road became crucial during the American Civil War.

evidence.claim: The Staunton-Parkersburg Turnpike byway crosses high mountains and valleys through Monongahela National Forest.
evidence.quote: Traveling over high mountains and secluded valleys, the byway traverses the Monongahela National Forest

evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration highlights woods, small farms, mountain views and Civil War sites along this National Scenic Byway.
evidence.quote: Staunton-Parkersburg Turnpike National Scenic Byway • West Virginia

evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration highlights woods, small farms, mountain views and Civil War sites along this National Scenic Byway.
evidence.quote: this road now features pristine Civil War sites and charming historic towns.

evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration highlights woods, small farms, mountain views and Civil War sites along this National Scenic Byway.
evidence.quote: woods, small farms and beautiful mountain vistas

evidence.claim: Its 180-mile West Virginia corridor runs from Parkersburg to just beyond Bartow.
evidence.quote: the Staunton-Parkersburg Turnpike (180 miles) from Parkersburg to just beyond Bartow.

evidence.claim: The federal byway page suggests two days to enjoy the route.
evidence.quote: Two days to enjoy the byway.

evidence.claim: The eastern mountain section follows a route of switchbacks and loops laid out by Crozet, with the byway guide identifying access to Civil War camps and battlefields.
evidence.quote: As the route winds through the mountainous terrain, there are many switchbacks and loops designed by Crozet

evidence.claim: The eastern mountain section follows a route of switchbacks and loops laid out by Crozet, with the byway guide identifying access to Civil War camps and battlefields.
evidence.quote: Provides access to numerous significant Civil War sites, such as Rich Mountain Battlefield, Cheat Summit Fort, Camp Bartow and Camp Allegheny

evidence.claim: The original turnpike had a longer ambition: connecting Staunton and the upper Shenandoah Valley with the Ohio River at Parkersburg.
evidence.quote: to provide a roadway from Staunton, Virginia and the upper Shenandoah Valley to the Ohio River at present-day Parkersburg, West Virginia.

evidence.claim: Virginia authorized construction funding in 1838, and engineer Claudius Crozet revised his earlier plans for the mountain crossing.
evidence.quote: After funding was authorized to build the turnpike in 1838, Crozet reviewed the earlier plans and revised some portions.

evidence.claim: Toll houses collected payment from local and through traffic.
evidence.quote: Toll houses, always staffed, were established at intervals, so as to collect from both types of traffic.

evidence.claim: During the Civil War, early campaigns sought control of the road and the nearby Baltimore and Ohio Railroad.
evidence.quote: some of the earliest campaigns of the Civil War were fought for control of the Staunton–Parkersburg (S-P) Turnpike, as well as the adjacent portion of the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad (B&O).

evidence.claim: As railroads expanded, through traffic became less important; in the 1920s, the state paved many roads for automobiles while retaining sections of the turnpike.
evidence.quote: While through-traffic along the turnpike became less important than in the past to local needs it remained an important thoroughfare.

evidence.claim: As railroads expanded, through traffic became less important; in the 1920s, the state paved many roads for automobiles while retaining sections of the turnpike.
evidence.quote: Beginning primarily in the boom years of the 1920s, the state paved many highways to provide for automobiles. Although the state made some re-routing improvements, considerable sections of the original turnpike remained the best available route through the state.

evidence.claim: As railroads expanded, through traffic became less important; in the 1920s, the state paved many roads for automobiles while retaining sections of the turnpike.
evidence.quote: By the end of the 19th century, virtually every hollow in West Virginia was reached by railroad lines.

evidence.claim: Drive east from Parkersburg on WV 47 to Linn, then follow US 33 through Weston and Buckhannon to Elkins.
evidence.quote: following West Virginia Route 47 east from Parkersburg to Linn, then U.S. Route 33 east through Weston and Buckhannon to Elkins

evidence.claim: US 250 continues southeast through Beverly and Huttonsville, crosses Cheat Mountain and reaches Bartow on the East Fork Greenbrier River.
evidence.quote: then U.S. Route 250 southeast through Beverly, Huttonsville

evidence.claim: US 250 continues southeast through Beverly and Huttonsville, crosses Cheat Mountain and reaches Bartow on the East Fork Greenbrier River.
evidence.quote: Cheat Mountain is crossed (east/west) by two federal highways: U.S. Route 33 in its northern third and U.S. Route 250 in its southern third.

evidence.claim: US 250 continues southeast through Beverly and Huttonsville, crosses Cheat Mountain and reaches Bartow on the East Fork Greenbrier River.
evidence.quote: Bartow is situated along U.S. Route 250 and West Virginia Route 92 and on the East Fork Greenbrier River

evidence.claim: The old turnpike crossed White Top, but modern US 250 skirts the knob beside Shavers Fork.
evidence.quote: While White Top was originally crossed by the Staunton–Parkersburg Turnpike, modern-day U.S. Route 250 skirts the base of the knob beside Shavers Fork to the north and east.

evidence.claim: The turnpike reached Beverly in 1841, and the town grew rapidly as a center of transport and trade.
evidence.quote: After the Staunton-Parkersburg Turnpike arrived (1841), the town developed rapidly as a regional center for transportation and trading.

evidence.claim: During the Civil War, both armies occupied it at different times, using buildings as hospitals and quarters.
evidence.quote: Both sides occupied Beverly at various times during the American Civil War (1861–65) and various buildings were pressed into service as hospitals or quarters.

evidence.claim: Beverly had served as county seat since 1790, but lost that role to Elkins in 1899 as the railroad and timbering center developed.
evidence.quote: Beverly was the county seat of Randolph County for over a century—from 1790 until 1899

evidence.claim: Beverly had served as county seat since 1790, but lost that role to Elkins in 1899 as the railroad and timbering center developed.
evidence.quote: Beverly lost its preeminence as county seat in 1899 to the rapidly developing railroad and timbering center of Elkins.

evidence.claim: The transfer of the county seat followed multiple referendums and court judgments; armed groups mobilized in both towns, but bloodshed was averted.
evidence.quote: This was resolved, however, only after multiple referendums, court judgments, and the mobilization of armed bands in both towns. In the end, bloodshed was averted.

evidence.claim: The town became a historic district in 1980, and a number of its historic structures have been restored.
evidence.quote: In 1980 the entire town was entered on the National Register of Historic Places as a historic district. Today, a number of Beverly’s more historic structures have been restored.

evidence.claim: Cheat Summit Fort stood above the old turnpike on White Top, guarding the approach to the Tygart Valley.
evidence.quote: Fort Milroy, also known as Cheat Summit Fort, offered an excellent view of the surrounding area including the Staunton-Parkersburg Turnpike which crossed about 100 feet (30 m) below the fort.  In guarding the Turnpike, Fort

evidence.claim: Cheat Summit Fort stood above the old turnpike on White Top, guarding the approach to the Tygart Valley.
evidence.quote: Milroy helped to guard entrance to the Tygart Valley River valley to the west.

evidence.claim: Construction began in July 1861.
evidence.quote: Construction on Fort Milroy (named for Union Brigadier General Robert H. Milroy) began on July 16, 1861.

evidence.claim: The camp account records snow on August 13 and horses freezing to death in mid-September during its first year of occupation.
evidence.quote: Snow was first reported for the year on August 13.  Horses froze to death in mid-September.

evidence.claim: Mountain weather and strategic changes contributed to its abandonment in April 1862.
evidence.quote: Cheat Summit Fort (Fort Milroy) was occupied from July 16, 1861, until April 1862 when it was abandoned due to extremes of weather as well as strategic developments.

evidence.claim: A cemetery lay south of the fort; after the war, all bodies were exhumed, with many reburied at the national cemetery in Grafton.
evidence.quote: A cemetery for those who died at Fort Milroy was built just south of the fort.  All bodies were exhumed from the site after the Civil War ended with many being reinterred at West Virginia National Cemetery in Grafton.

evidence.claim: Depressions from the graves remain visible, marking the former burial ground.
evidence.quote: Depressions from the graves are still visible today.

evidence.claim: Confederate troops occupied Allegheny Mountain’s summit pass to defend the turnpike and its approach to the Shenandoah Valley.
evidence.quote: Confederate forces under Col. Edward Johnson occupied the summit pass of Allegheny Mountain (roughly 4,400 feet above sea level)  to defend the  Staunton and Parkersburg Turnpike that offered a point of access from the mountains of western Virginia into the strategic Shenandoah Valley.

evidence.claim: On December 13, 1861, Union troops attacked in two columns.
evidence.quote: The next morning, Milroy divided his troops into a two pronged attack to flank the Confederate camp.

evidence.claim: On December 13, 1861, Union troops attacked in two columns.
evidence.quote: The Battle of Camp Allegheny, also known as the Battle of Allegheny Mountain, took place on December 13, 1861

evidence.claim: Difficult terrain delayed the second column until the first had withdrawn, preventing the planned support.
evidence.quote: Because of the difficult mountain terrain, the second Union column arrived shortly after the withdrawal of the first column, therefore unable to support the main body of Union troops on the right as planned

evidence.claim: The Union attack failed, and the Confederate force remained through winter.
evidence.quote: the failed Union assault convinced the Confederate higher command to reinforce Johnson's force in place at Camp Allegheny with five regiments through the remainder of the harsh winter of 1861–62.

evidence.claim: Losses through the mountain winter and the difficulty of supplying the remote post contributed to the decision to abandon it in April 1862.
evidence.quote: Combined with the loss of men in the harsh mountain winter and the logistical challenges of keeping the remote mountain post effectively supplied, General Robert E. Lee agreed to let Johnson abandon the post in favor of Shenandoah Mountain on April 2, 1862.

evidence.claim: The historic district includes earthworks, a cemetery, and the sites of huts, a church and the Yeager farmstead.
evidence.quote: They are the earthworks, site of hut and campground, cemetery, church site, and the site of the Yeager farmstead.

flags: The road-history cache quotes a four-degree grade specification but later calls it four percent. The original specification is not cached independently; numerical grade omitted.
Current overstates the December battle as alone keeping Highland County in Virginia. The cache also invokes the later McDowell battle and the statehood bill. That simplified causal claim is removed.
Beverly’s oldest-settlement superlative is not supported by a community or primary history, and the same page describes earlier settlement. It is omitted.
The 43-mile state-guide entry covers a narrower or older corridor than the 180-mile national byway in FHWA and e-WV. Use 180 miles for the byway; the historic toll road extended to Staunton.

Battlefield backways are described as largely unpaved by the state program, but the cached guide lacks the referenced site-specific pages. No current access or road-surface guarantee is made for the excursions.
The gold-payment anecdote is supported by a secondary cache page but omitted for focus. Camp-weather details are presented as a camp account; no primary battle or camp account is cached.
